name: tier1_wall_review
_comment: THE WALL GATE SCENE — tier one, the round that retires the magenta mocks.
It is a fifth spec rather than an edit to a fourth for the reason already recorded on the
third and the fourth: every existing spec is cited by evidence on disk, and changing one
silently invalidates every comparison ever taken through it.
WHAT IT MUST CONTAIN, and each item is here to be ANSWERED rather than to be present.
The four contexts are the ones the gate's own questions need:
1. SOUTH REVEALS AT MORE THAN ONE RANGE. Bible §3 says a tile shows a front face exactly
where floor lies south, and §6.2.1 asks whether §6.5's value stack survives the falloff
ACROSS the lit radius rather than at its middle. A scene whose only reveal sits three
tiles from the lamp answers the second question at one point and reports it as the
answer. So there are reveals at ONE tile (the island, and the chokepoint's own jambs),
at THREE (the masses' south faces) and at FIVE-PLUS (room B's north wall, past the
delivered reach).
2. A CHOKEPOINT BETWEEN TWO MASSES. One tile wide, two deep, at x=8. The gate asks
whether it reads as a PASSAGE BETWEEN MASSES rather than as a gap in a pattern, and
that question needs two masses with real thickness either side of it — not a corridor
cut through solid rock, which is what every previous wall scene had.
3. CORNERS, BOTH KINDS. The chokepoint's mouths give four INNER corners (wall wrapping
around floor). The island at (5,15) gives four OUTER ones (floor wrapping around wall),
which is the case §3's two-plane rule is hardest on: an outer corner is where a wall
stops, and if the planes do not turn with it the mass reads as a card.
4. WALL SEEN AT A GLANCE, NOT ONLY UP CLOSE. Room B sits north of the chokepoint and
partly outside the delivered reach (§6.2's note: the ratified radius is 5.0 tiles and
the lamp's delivered reach is about four). The arc is part of the distribution, and a
scene where every wall is legible is not the game.
THE PLAYER STANDS AT (8,15), in room A, four tiles south of the chokepoint's mouth. The
island is two tiles away, the masses' south faces are four, and room B's far wall is nine.
THE FLOOR IS THE LANDED ASHLAR FAMILY and is not under review here. What is under review is
the wall standing on it, the void beyond it, and whether the three read as one place.
_legibility: Distances are from the player at (8,15) and the ratified radius is 5.0 TILES (Ruling 56),
whose DELIVERED reach is about four (§6.2.1's nominal-vs-delivered note). The lit points are
therefore declared no further out than four, and the dark ones past five — the fifth tile is
the ambiguous band and nothing is asserted about it in either direction.
Every point is a FLOOR cell inside the dungeon view (0,90)..(750,1001). ProbeFloorLegibility

_carve_note: Row 15 is carved in two pieces either side of x=5, which leaves ONE CELL STANDING at (5,15).
That is the island: floor on all four sides and on all four diagonals, so it is the only
geometry in any review scene that puts an outer corner on every side of the same mass.
The band at y=6..11 is NOT carved except at x=8, so the two masses either side of the
chokepoint are the full width of the map and SIX cells deep. Six rather than three, and the
reason is a defect this scene had in its first form: the wall system draws two rings of
stone and then the void, so a three-deep mass is ring 1 and ring 2 and nothing else, and the
scene DID NOT CONTAIN THE VOID IT EXISTS TO RULE ON. Measured: 66 void cells in the map and
none of them inside the dungeon view. A scene that cannot pose its own question is the
failure §2.2 asks every capture to declare, arriving one level up.
Two rings of stone is itself derived rather than chosen: WALL-RECIPE §2.2 measured every room
boundary in the asset bar at two tiles or more, and §7.4 gives the register - a held line is
thick because thickness is what holding costs.
The stub at x1..2, y16..17 is a neglected side passage off room A's west wall, carried over
from the floor gate scene for the same reason it exists there: §8.2's polish-means-on-path
says nothing unless some floor in frame is off the path. It is short on purpose so it cannot
become the map's longest through-route and get treaded.
